source_read: PDF, pp. 383–389 (all 7 pages read; Figures 1–4 checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi; Figures 2 and 3 also read from a 300-dpi crop for bar heights)

claims.overstatement: None in the numbers. Wording risk: 'relatively lower metabolism in the thalamus (17%) and striatum (6–12%)' is correct only as region-to-global ratios. In absolute terms (Figure 2) users' caudate metabolism was about equal to controls' and putamen about 8% higher, thalamus about 4% lower. The relative decreases arise largely from dividing by a higher global value. Suggest the claim say so explicitly, e.g. 'lower only after normalizing to the higher whole-brain value'.
claims.note: Checked: 38.4 vs 33.6 µmol/100 g/min gives +14.3%; my t from the printed means and SDs is 2.2 (df=34), two-tailed p≈0.035, which fails the paper's own p<0.01 threshold (Methods, p. 384). My standardized difference: about 0.75 (95% CI roughly 0.06 to 1.43). Relative values read from Figure 3 match the text: thalamus −17%, caudate −11.5%, putamen −6%, parietal +5.5%; they are consistent with Figure 2 absolute values divided by the global means. Smoking 73% vs 24% and women 60% vs 28% (6/21 is 28.6%) confirmed. Cognition in users only confirmed. 'Another research group found no difference' (London et al., 2004) does not come from this source.

anchors.extracted: Global metabolism 38.4 (SD 8) in 15 users vs 33.6 (SD 5) µmol/100 g/min in 21 controls, 14% higher, t=2.2, df=34, p<0.05. Absolute parietal 20% higher (Figure 2 footnote: t=2.9, df=34, p<0.01). Frontal, temporal, occipital cortex and hippocampus higher (text: 11–12%; t 2.0–2.4, p<0.05) but described as not significant.

anchors.locator: Method › Image and Data Analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Significance threshold for group and correlation tests set at p<0.01 to correct for multiple comparisons (between 0.05 and the Bonferroni value of 0.005). SPM maps at p<0.005, uncorrected, with clusters of at least 250 pixels.

Normalized to global: parietal 5% higher (t=3.7, p<0.001); thalamus 17%, caudate 12% (single footnote for both: t=5.5, p<0.0001) and putamen 6% (t=2.7, p<0.01) lower. Group × region (caudate vs putamen) interaction F(1,34)=4.8, p<0.05.

Read from bar heights: users vs controls, thalamus about 43.8 vs 45.8 (about −4%), caudate about 45.8 vs 45.5 (no difference), putamen about 50.7 vs 46.9 (about +8%). Subcortical decreases are therefore relative to the elevated global value, not absolute.

Users 6 men/9 women, age 32, from Los Angeles rehabilitation centres; 12 tested 2 weeks–5 months and 3 tested 11–35 months after last use. Controls 15 men/6 women, age 31, by advertisement. Women 60% vs 28%. Women only (9 vs 6): higher whole-brain (t=2.2, df=13, p<0.05) and lower relative thalamus and caudate; men only (6 vs 15): lower relative thalamus, caudate, putamen; whole-brain result for men not reported (data not shown).

Smokers 73% of users vs 24% of controls; users probably used more alcohol and cannabis; time since last use self-reported in outpatients; HIV not tested in controls; neurocognitive tests given only to users, so group differences in cognition cannot be determined.

The 3 users abstinent 11 months or longer: relative caudate 12% lower than controls (t=3.6, df=22, p<0.002); global 13% higher and relative thalamus 10% lower, not significant. No metabolic measure correlated with days since last use.

Consider adding that the subcortical decreases are relative only: in absolute values (Figure 2, p. 385) caudate was about equal and putamen about 8% higher in users.
Data correct, but this is the Results' 2nd paragraph (p. 385, left column, starting 'To assess if there was any evidence of recovery'), not the 3rd.

Data correct. The days-since-last-use result ends the Results' 2nd paragraph (p. 385, left column, running onto the right column); the absence of thalamic/striatal correlations with test scores is in the 3rd paragraph (p. 385, right column). reporting_issues.note: Threshold stated in Methods (p. 384); global result and the four 'not significant' regions on p. 384. The occipital t (2.4) is larger than the global t (2.2).
Parietal–pegboard r=0.73 and years-of-use r=−0.62, both df=14 (p. 385).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed. Add: the title and abstract describe 'lower subcortical metabolism', but this is lower only after normalizing to the elevated whole-brain value; absolute caudate and putamen values were not lower (Figure 2, p. 385).

missed: Figure 2 (p. 385): in absolute terms, users' thalamic metabolism was about 4% lower, caudate about equal and putamen about 8% higher than controls'. The relative decreases (Figure 3) follow from dividing by a 14% higher global value. This matters for how the encyclopedia words 'lower striatal metabolism'.

Reporting issue: the text gives 11–12% higher absolute metabolism for frontal, temporal, occipital cortex and hippocampus (p. 384), but Figure 2 bars indicate roughly 13%, 12%, 17% and 17% (approximate bar readings, p. 385).
Reporting issue: Figure 3's footnote c assigns one test statistic (t=5.5, p<0.0001) to two regions (thalamus and caudate) (p. 385).

Sex-stratified analysis (p. 386): whole-brain elevation is reported for women only (9 vs 6); the men's whole-brain result is not reported ('data not shown'), so 'findings consistent' is not fully documented.

Whole-brain metabolism correlated negatively with years of use (r=−0.62; not significant after age adjustment), i.e. opposite in direction to the users-higher group difference; not discussed (p. 385).

The Discussion compares the pattern with atypical parkinsonism rather than idiopathic Parkinson's disease (equal caudate and putamen DAT loss; lower thalamic and striatal metabolism) (p. 387). This is relevant to the encyclopedia's claim on the Parkinson's pattern (cl_meth_dopamine_damage).

Minor: reference 18 cites the companion DAT paper with a different title and pages 384–390 instead of 377–382 (p. 388). The abstinence ranges differ slightly from the companion paper (2 weeks–5 months and 11–35 months here, 2–24 weeks and 11–36 months in 2001a).
